strengths: Clear insight into local vs. global representations for ODE inference, effectively demonstrated with the frictionless pendulum vs. CDIMA example
Impressive parameter and data efficiency: achieves comparable performance to ODEFormer with 10× fewer parameters and 80× less training data
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple regimes (synthetic, low-data, real-world) with extensive ablations and statistical analysis
Excellent reproducibility: detailed appendices cover data generation, architecture, hyperparameters, and promised code release
Honest and thorough treatment of limitations, with concrete identification of failure modes and future directions
weaknesses: Critical limitation to d ≤ 3 dimensions severely restricts practical applicability; most realistic dynamical systems are higher-dimensional, and the non-stationary polynomial prior issue is identified but unsolved

Zero-shot performance claims are overstated: real-world results (MoCap, low-data regimes) require finetuning; Table 4's 'selected noise' results cherry-pick favorable noise realizations, and Table 7 shows massive variance (0.017–4.756 MSE across 100 seeds)
Generalization performance (Table 2, ~27–32% success rate) is comparable to or worse than ODEFormer, undermining the claimed advantages
Unfair model comparison: FIM-ODE (8M params) vs. ODEFormer (86M params) makes it unclear whether gains stem from simpler prior or model scale; no size-controlled ablations
Pretraining prior has unresolved issues: non-stationary variance scaling (Figures 3–5) causes trajectory divergence requiring filtering that biases training toward 'well-behaved' dynamics
MoCap experiments show dramatic failures for subjects 35/39 (655.4 MSE) vs. subject 09 (6.1 MSE) when discarded PCA components carry important dynamics, revealing practical limitations
Limited architectural novelty: neural operator design largely adapted from Seifner et al. (2025a); incremental improvements over existing work
Incomplete failure mode analysis: frictionless pendulum failure identified but not systematized; unclear guidance on when to use FIM-ODE vs. alternatives

strengths: Clear motivation for local vector field representations with effective illustrations (Figure 2)
Strong zero-shot trajectory reconstruction on ODEBench (84.4% vs 63.1% for ODEformer at σ=0.0, ρ=0.0)
Parameter and data efficiency: achieves comparable performance with ~10x fewer parameters and ~80x fewer training systems
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple regimes (synthetic, low-data, real-world) with extensive ablations
Honest and detailed discussion of fundamental limitations (dimensionality curse, non-stationary prior issues)
Well-structured presentation with clear writing and thorough appendices
weaknesses: Severe dimensionality limitation (d ≤ 3) is fundamental, not solvable in future work: non-stationary polynomial prior causes curse of dimensionality and trajectory divergence; greatly restricts real-world applicability

Mixed generalization results undermine claims: trajectory generalization (Table 2) shows comparable, not superior performance to ODEformer at R²>0.9 threshold; out-of-distribution to degree-6 polynomials shows significant drops (26.0%→15.0% for generalization)

Low-data regime results are disappointing: zero-shot performance on VDP/FHN significantly underperforms classical methods (e.g., MSE 0.89 vs 0.03 for GP-DNF); extreme noise sensitivity (Table 7: std dev up to 1.988)

Real-world validation limited and problematic: human motion experiments fail on 2/3 subjects without finetuning (655.40, 48.94 MSE vs 6.72 for GP-DNF); only works when 3D projection retains ~94% variance
Finetuning undermines amortization motivation: all competitive results require task-specific training; no quantification of finetuning cost vs training classical methods from scratch

Limited technical novelty: architecture adapted from Seifner et al. (2025a), FIM framework established, polynomial prior is straightforward; core contribution is incremental application to polynomial ODEs

Restrictive and poorly justified polynomial prior: only degree ≤ 3, no validation on diverse real systems; Appendix B.4 reveals systematic bias with vector field magnitudes concentrating near boundaries
Evaluation concerns: R²>0.9 is stringent (Table 6 at R²>0.8 more favorable); missing SINDy/symbolic regression comparisons; reporting 'best seed' results for VDP/FHN obscures actual variability
Code unavailable at review time ('will be released shortly'); reproducibility details for uncertainty weighting loss and hyperparameter choices incomplete
Presentation issues: claims 'matching and often improving upon ODEformer' are overstated given mixed generalization results; key limitations (d≤3, non-stationary prior) understated in main text

strengths: Well-motivated core insight: local neural operator representations outperform global symbolic expressions, with clear intuition and concrete examples (Figure 2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three distinct regimes (zero-shot, low-data with finetuning, real-world data) with extensive ablations and honest acknowledgment of limitations

Exceptional reproducibility: thorough appendices with architecture details, training hyperparameters, loss curves, data generation procedures, and extensive ablations on dataset size, discretization, and vector field quality metrics
Practical contribution: enables practitioners to perform zero-shot ODE inference without ML expertise; rapid finetuning outperforms classical baselines; code to be released

Technically sound design choices: thoughtful transition-based input features, scale normalization across systems with different magnitudes, uncertainty-weighted heteroscedastic loss appropriately handling variable flow magnitudes
Efficient model: 13M parameters achieving competitive or superior performance to 86M-parameter ODEFormer trained on 50M systems vs. 0.6M systems
Robust generalization beyond training prior: demonstrates local representations can transfer to non-polynomial systems (trigonometric, rational functions) despite polynomial-only pretraining
Clear, well-written presentation with informative figures and comprehensive discussion of trade-offs
weaknesses: Fundamental dimensionality limitation: restriction to d≤3 significantly constrains practical applicability; motion capture experiments had to project 50D→3D, losing 7.7%-5.1% of variance for some subjects, with zero-shot performance degrading catastrophically (MSE 655.40 vs baseline ~7-19)

Mixed experimental results not fully consistent with abstract claims of 'strong zero-shot performance': Table 2 shows no consistent advantage over ODEFormer on generalization (27.0% vs 31.1% at some settings); Table 4 shows zero-shot failure in low-data regime requiring finetuning; Table 5 shows zero-shot human motion capture failure

Noise sensitivity undermines zero-shot reliability: Table 7 reveals striking sensitivity to noise realization with standard deviations of 0.687-1.988 and ranges spanning 0.017-11.502, indicating brittleness in practical applications

Insufficient ablation and unfair comparison: ODEFormer trained on 50M vs 0.6M systems (83× difference); different priors make it unclear whether improvements stem from neural operators or simpler distribution; missing ablation comparing same architecture with ODEFormer's prior

Limited analysis of failure modes: no investigation of which system properties lead to good vs poor predictions; no theoretical explanation for why local representations work; high sensitivity to noise realization not sufficiently analyzed

Pretraining prior limitations: polynomial degree ≤3 may not generalize to qualitatively different systems; non-stationary scaling (||x||^(2α) behavior) creates fundamental numerical challenges causing trajectory divergence, addressed only through filtering rather than design

Insufficient architectural justification: limited ablations on transformer design choices (2-layer encoder, 8-layer decoder); uncertainty weighting via auxiliary head never validated for calibration; loss function choice (MAE) not compared to dynamics-aware alternatives

Main text downplays limitations: critical caveats about noise sensitivity, poor generalization, and real-world performance failures relegated to appendices or briefly mentioned; readers may have inflated expectations from abstract

strengths: Impressive efficiency gains: 10× smaller model and 80× less training data than ODEFormer while maintaining competitive performance on reconstruction tasks

Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning synthetic benchmarks (ODEBench with ID/OOD analysis), low-data regimes (VDP/FHN with context size ablations), and real-world human motion capture with detailed finetuning analysis

Novel demonstration that local neural operator representations support interpretable dynamical systems analysis (equilibria, Jacobians, stability classification) comparable to symbolic methods, bridging local and global representation paradigms
Exceptional reproducibility documentation with extensive appendices detailing architecture, training procedures, hyperparameters, ablations, and implementation details; code and tutorials promised

Honest and thorough limitations discussion, acknowledging fundamental constraints (NP-hardness, non-identifiability, non-stationary prior scaling, curse of dimensionality) and their practical implications
weaknesses: Critical dimensionality limitation: Restriction to d≤3 due to non-stationary prior scaling and trajectory divergence severely constrains practical applicability; many real scientific systems operate in higher dimensions, and the paper offers no concrete solution beyond vague future work on 'stationary GP constructions'

Poor zero-shot performance in realistic low-data regimes: Table 4 shows FIM-ODE achieves 0.90 MSE vs. 0.03 for GP-DNF on VDP Task 1 (30× worse); high variance across noise realizations with acknowledged inability to constrain dynamics; undermines zero-shot premise since practitioners must finetune anyway

Overstated comparison to ODEFormer: Trajectory generalization performance (Table 2) is comparable, not clearly better; improvements at R²>0.8 (5-10%) lack statistical significance testing and may be within noise; different priors and training scales (50M vs 0.6M systems) confound comparison

Severely limited real-world validation: Only motion capture tested with heavy preprocessing (PCA to 3 dimensions artificially aligns data to model constraints); only 3 subjects with catastrophic failures on 2 subjects (MSE 295-655) without finetuning; no evidence of generalization across scientific domains

Methodological issue in finetuning experiments: Section D.1 acknowledges using held-out test-window MSE for checkpoint selection, creating circular reasoning on held-out data ('does not constitute fully independent test protocol'); undermines confidence in finetuning results shown as primary contribution

Weak statistical rigor: No confidence intervals or significance tests on most comparisons; Table 4 high standard deviations (0.8(7)) suggest results may be within noise; Tables 1-2 report percentages without confidence intervals, making it unclear if differences are significant

Unjustified design choices: Transition-based input representation [Δy, Δy², Δτ] lacks ablation justification; 50/50 mixed sampling strategy has no sensitivity analysis; uncertainty weighting loss borrowed from FIM-SDE without justification versus alternatives (curriculum learning, importance weighting)

Fundamental prior construction issues: Non-stationary scaling (Var(f(x))∝||x||^{2α}) creates distribution mismatch between initial condition sampling N(0,1) and vector field magnitudes; trajectory filtering (discarding ||x||>10²) biases prior toward well-behaved dynamics; design choices feel ad-hoc

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation including ODEBench, low-data regimes, real-world motion capture, extensive ablations, and detailed appendices demonstrating thorough investigation
Novel interpretability analysis showing neural operators can be queried for dynamical systems properties (equilibria, Jacobians, stability), extending beyond typical black-box approaches
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations, including non-stationary prior issues, dimensionality constraints, and architectural fixed-dimensionality design choices
Strong effort toward reproducibility with promised code release, tutorials, pretrained models, and detailed hyperparameter documentation
Clear motivation for the research question: whether simpler pretraining priors can achieve good generalization compared to more complex symbolic priors
weaknesses: Fundamental dimensionality limitation (d ≤ 3) remains unresolved despite being called a primary constraint. Non-stationary polynomial prior causes divergence; paper defers solution to future work rather than implementing stationary GP alternative. This severely limits practical applicability to real-world problems requiring higher dimensions (molecular dynamics, climate modeling, protein folding)

Zero-shot performance fails in practical low-data regimes (Table 4): FIM-ODE achieves 0.90 MSE vs classical baselines like GP-DNF at 0.03 MSE for VDP T1. Only after finetuning (0.028 MSE) does it compete, undermining foundation model value proposition and suggesting marginal advantage over training from scratch

Unfair comparison with ODEFormer confounds multiple factors: ODEFormer uses 86M parameters vs 8M, trained on 50M systems vs 0.6M, with more complex prior. Table 10 shows FIM-ODE achieves only 16.7% success on 3D ID systems vs 93.3% on 2D—3D performance is essentially non-functional

Out-of-distribution generalization limitations revealed by Table 2 and Figure 2: both methods collapse on generalization tasks (<33% success). Critical failure case (frictionless pendulum) shows FIM-ODE converts marginal centers into unstable spirals, destroying conservative structure that ODEFormer preserves. Local representation cannot enforce global geometric constraints

Interpretability claims overstate results (Table 13): equilibrium residuals reach 0.68, stability types are incorrect (pendulum), and recovered equilibria are spatially distorted. These are not interpretable in the dynamical systems sense—they lack the exactness that enables reliable analysis

Limited real-world validation with mixed results: only CMU Motion Capture tested. Subjects 35 and 39 fail dramatically without finetuning (MSE 655.40 and 295.29 zero-shot), suggesting polynomial prior is highly restrictive. Restriction to 3D latent space (zeroing higher PCs) is artificial rather than exploring natural dimensionality

Methodological violation in finetuning experiments (Appendix D.1): best checkpoints for VDP/FHN are selected on held-out test window rather than validation set, violating standard ML practice and inflating reported performance. Paper acknowledges but proceeds anyway

Technical novelty is incremental: foundation inference model framework from prior work (FIM-SDE, FIM for Markov chains), neural operator architecture adapted directly from FIM-SDE, only the polynomial ODE prior is novel. This is primarily an application contribution rather than methodological advance

Incomplete experimental justification: trained on 600k systems while Appendix G.3 shows diminishing returns beyond 100k. No analysis of computational cost vs performance tradeoff. Dataset size choices appear unmotivated

Presentation overclaiming contradicted by results: Abstract claims 'strong zero-shot performance' but Table 4 demonstrates zero-shot failure in low-data regimes. Claims of 'improving upon ODEFormer' are context-dependent and confounded by experimental design choices

strengths: Strong empirical efficiency: Matches or exceeds much larger baseline (ODEFormer) with 10× fewer parameters and 80× fewer training systems, demonstrating value of simpler priors
Well-motivated design choices: Polynomial pretraining, transition-based representations, uncertainty weighting, and mixed sampling strategy are all justified and effective

Interpretability without sacrificing performance: Demonstrates neural operator vector fields can be queried for equilibria, Jacobians, and stability analysis while maintaining or improving over symbolic baselines

Comprehensive evaluation: Multiple experimental settings (reconstruction, generalization, forecasting, imputation, real-world), extensive ablations, honest ID/OOD analysis, and clear failure case analysis
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed implementation appendices (C-D), training statistics, explicit acknowledgment of limitations (D.1 checkpoint selection), and promised code release
Clear presentation: Well-organized paper with honest limitations discussion, appropriate impact statement, and careful treatment of fundamental non-identifiability issues
weaknesses: Severe dimensional scalability limitation: Restricted to d≤3 with catastrophic performance degradation in 3D (16.7% reconstruction vs 92.3% in 2D). Non-stationary polynomial prior creates fundamental curse of dimensionality; future work needed to address this

Overstated zero-shot claims: Motion capture shows dramatic failures without finetuning (655.40 MSE on subjects 35-39 vs 6.10 for subject 09); VDP has high variance (0.8±7). Primary utility is as initialization rather than plug-and-play inference

Fundamental local-global tradeoff: Cannot preserve global structure (e.g., conservative geometry in pendulum, Figure 2). Produces physically incorrect equilibria (Table 13 residuals 10^-2 to 10^-1). Interpretability claims weakened when practitioners cannot distinguish correct from incorrect inferred structures

Training data bias from distribution design: Non-stationary prior with filtering of divergent trajectories (|x|>10²) creates selection bias. High variance in vector field magnitudes near boundaries (Figures 4-6) introduces systematic training artifact
Incremental novelty: Primarily adapts existing FIM-SDE framework to deterministic setting rather than proposing new methodology. While execution is solid, the conceptual contribution is limited

Insufficient analysis of failure modes and guidance: Paper shows when method fails (high-D, OOD dynamics, motion capture subjects) but doesn't provide practitioners with diagnostics or heuristics for predicting success/failure on new problems
